### Supporting basis

Zstandard level 3 significantly outperforms gzip level 6 in decompression speed, which is critical given your workflow of repeated reads. While both algorithms produce comparable compressed sizes for 1 KB JSON records with repeated fields, Zstd’s dictionary compression excels at identifying common structures like field names and timestamps. Gzip level 6 offers a reasonable compromise between compression ratio and speed but lacks Zstd’s optimized decompression pipeline. Since you compress once and decompress many times, the slight increase in compression time for Zstd is negligible compared to the cumulative time saved during repeated extraction. Practical benchmarks show Zstd level 3 decompression speeds are often 2-4 times faster than gzip level 6, while maintaining similar or slightly better compression ratios for structured text data. This performance asymmetry strongly favors Zstd in read-heavy scenarios where storage space is not the primary constraint.

### Recommendation

Choose Zstandard level 3. Your primary constraint is read throughput, as you will decompress the archives repeatedly. Zstandard provides superior decompression performance without sacrificing significant space efficiency compared to gzip level 6. For 10 GB of JSON logs with repetitive patterns, Zstd will likely achieve a similar or slightly smaller archive size due to better dictionary modeling of repeated keys. Since compression occurs only once, the marginally higher CPU cost for Zstd is irrelevant. The substantial gain in decompression speed directly improves operational efficiency for log analysis or replay tasks. Unless you have extremely strict storage limitations where every byte of gzip’s marginal compression advantage outweighs all other factors, Zstandard is the optimal choice. It balances space and speed effectively, prioritizing the frequent read operations that define your use case.<|im_end|>
